papers.title: Sex-specific skeletal ageing trajectories and reference centiles across vertebrae and ribs in over 78,000 patients
papers.abstract: Background Age-related bone loss is well established, but CT attenuation trajectories across the skeleton are poorly characterised. Automated segmentation makes every bone measurable, yet site-specific trajectories, and interchangeability with the conventionally used L1, remain unclear. Methods In this retrospective multicentre cross-sectional study we analysed non-contrast torso CT performed during 2024 at nine Japanese academic hospitals in the Japan Medical Image Database. Patients aged 15-100 years with abdominopelvic coverage were eligible, one examination each. Mean attenuation of 25 vertebrae and 24 ribs was measured from TotalSegmentator v2.10.0 masks. The main outcome was the age- and sex-specific distribution of attenuation at each site. We fitted sex-specific spline mean curves and quantile-regression centiles, tested the sex-by-age interaction, and assessed each site as an L1 surrogate by age-adjusted correlation, errors-in-variables conversion, and discrimination of low-for-age L1. Findings Of 239 766 examinations from 135 425 patients, 79 482 remained after restricting to torso coverage and one examination per patient, and 78 620 after 862 exclusions for age or sex (41 056 men, 37 564 women; mean age 65.3 [SD 15.8] years). Attenuation fell with age at all 49 sites in women and 46 of 49 in men, with a sex-dependent shape everywhere (all FDR-adjusted p<0.0001). Female decline was steepest at a median of 52.0 years, and the 40-80-year change was a median -34.1% versus -12.8% in men. L2 reproduced L1 closely (limits of agreement +/-45 HU); ribs did not (+/-68 to +/-82 HU). Interpretation These centiles place an automated attenuation measurement at any of 49 sites against age- and sex-matched peers. Vertebrae adjacent to L1 may replace it with a stated precision; ribs may not.

papers.title: Lesion selection and external evaluation of clinical-imaging survival models after transarterial chemoembolization for hepatocellular carcinoma
papers.abstract: Background: Pretreatment computed tomography (CT) describes tumor characteristics in patients receiving transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), but whether measuring more tumors improves mortality predictions in a new cohort remains unclear. We assessed the added value of different lesion-selection scopes beyond shared clinical predictors. Methods: We compared a model using five clinical variables with models adding CT measurements from the largest, two largest, or all retained annotated tumors. All models used the same regularized discrete-time survival estimator. Evaluation used repeated nested cross-validation in 228 WAW-TACE patients and frozen external application in 69 HCC-TACE-Seg patients, with 15 deaths by day 365. We assessed first-year probability error, discrimination, and calibration, followed by local recalibration using small external samples. Results: Internally, adding CT-derived lesion features did not establish an improvement in prediction accuracy. Externally, the all-lesion model had the highest discrimination point estimates, but its advantage over the clinical-only model was uncertain. Its mortality probabilities were less accurate than those of the clinical-only model, with calibration estimates consistent with overly extreme predicted risks. Local recalibration reduced its median held-out prediction error at day 365, but the median adjusted error remained higher than that of the adjusted clinical model. Simple tumor-burden predictors also did not improve external probability accuracy over the clinical baseline. Conclusions: In these cohorts, measurements from more annotated tumors did not yield more reliable first-year mortality probabilities. Comparisons of clinical-imaging models should evaluate external probability accuracy and calibration alongside patient ranking.

papers.title: Fractional tumor burden refines prognostic stratification beyond MGMT status in glioblastoma after chemoradiotherapy
papers.abstract: Background and Purpose. Following standard-of-care treatment for glioblastoma, response to chemoradiotherapy is difficult to evaluate because changes on postcontrast T1WI may represent either treatment effect or tumor progression, particularly in the early posttreatment period. Although O6-methylguanine DNA methyltransferase promoter methylation is prognostic and informs treatment response, outcomes among patients remain heterogeneous. We hypothesized that combining advanced physiologic imaging with methylation status would improve early prognostic stratification. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective cohort study, patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma who underwent surgical resection or biopsy followed by standard chemoradiotherapy and had diffusion- and perfusion-weighted MR imaging within 6 weeks after treatment completion were included. Imaging-derived metrics included mean apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), mean standardized relative cerebral blood volume (sRCBV), change in contrast-enhancing volume on dT1, and the volume of fractional tumor burden (FTB), which is the volume of enhancing tissue with moderate-to-high probability of vascular tumor. Overall survival was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier analysis with log-rank testing. Results. Forty-three patients (21 male, 22 female) were included with a mean age of 57 years. Median overall survival was longer in patients with O6-methylguanine DNA methyltransferase-methylated tumors compared with unmethylated tumors (19.7 vs 10.6 months; P = .01). Stratification by mean sRCBV, mean ADC, or change in dT1 volumes was not associated with overall survival (P > .05 for all comparisons). Among unmethylated tumors, FTB <5 mL was associated with longer overall survival compared with [≥]5 mL (14.5 vs 8.4 months; P = .006), whereas no survival difference, based on FTB volumes, was observed in methylated tumors (P = .50). Conclusions. Fractional tumor burden, measured within 6 weeks after chemoradiotherapy, refines prognostic stratification beyond methylation status in glioblastoma, identifying a subgroup of unmethylated tumors with longer overall survival. These findings support the use of spatially resolved perfusion imaging to improve interpretation of early posttreatment enhancement.

papers.title: MedMLX: On-Device Medical Imaging AI for Apple Silicon
papers.abstract: Background: Medical imaging research increasingly combines specialized artificial intelligence models for segmentation, detection, image synthesis and report generation. For three-dimensional CT and MRI, these workflows typically run on NVIDIA GPUs with substantial memory. On-device AI on widely available Apple Silicon computers could broaden access to these models for clinical researchers. These computers share a large memory pool between the CPU and GPU, which suits workflows that combine several models. However, few established imaging models run natively on Apple Silicon. Adapting a model to new hardware also requires verifying that its results match the original software. Methods: We developed MedMLX, a collection of 21 established medical imaging models rewritten for Apple Silicon in MLX, Apple's machine learning framework. The collection includes nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator, MedSAM2 and SAM 3. The models segment organs and tumors, detect lung nodules, generate synthetic images and draft radiology reports from CT, MRI, PET/CT, radiographs and endoscopic images. Using public cases from 11 imaging datasets, we compared the models' results with those of the original software run on an Intel CPU and an NVIDIA GPU. Agreement required a Dice coefficient of at least 0.99 for every segmentation label and equivalent criteria for other outputs. We measured memory use and processing time on an Apple M1 Max computer with 64 GB of memory. Results: MedMLX agreed with the original software in 211 of 212 comparisons. The single exception was a brain MRI segmentation. On this case, the original software itself gave different results on the two devices. We illustrated sequential workflows, including anatomical segmentation of a synthetic brain MRI and lesion synthesis guided by organ segmentation. With a memory-saving setting, 19 of the 21 models used less than 16 GB of memory. This setting reduced memory use by a median of 49% and increased processing time by a median of 13%. Conclusions: MedMLX enables on-device AI with established medical imaging models on Apple Silicon computers rather than specialized NVIDIA hardware. The models agree closely with the original software, and most need less than 16 GB of memory.

papers.title: Development and evaluation of automated organ segmentation models for abdominal ultrasound in injured children
papers.abstract: Background: Accurate organ segmentation in pediatric focused assessment with sonography in trauma (FAST) is an important prerequisite for automated image analysis and image quality assessment, but manual segmentation is time-intensive, subject to inter- and intra-observer variability, and limits the scalability of deep learning dataset development. Although deep learning has shown promise for ultrasound organ segmentation, its application to pediatric FAST has not been evaluated. Objective: To describe the development and evaluation of deep learning models to automatically localize and segment six abdominal organs in pediatric FAST. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study using a convenience sample of archived FAST examinations from 200 injured children evaluated at a Level I pediatric trauma center. Emergency ultrasound fellowship-trained physicians manually segmented six key abdominal organs. Annotated image-mask pairs were split into training and test sets at 80:20. We developed or fine-tuned U-Net, EVIT U-Net, UltraSAM, and nnU-Net models to automatically segment the bladder, kidney, liver, spleen, spine, and diaphragm. Segmentation accuracy was assessed using the Dice-S&oslashrensen Coefficient (DSC) compared with manual annotations. Pediatric emergency ultrasound experts reviewed previously unlabeled FAST clips and rated the acceptability of model-generated organ masks. Results: The dataset included 1,807 manually annotated image-mask pairs from 200 pediatric FAST clips. Using an 80:20 split with no overlap between video clips, 1,446 image-mask pairs were used for training and 361 for testing. Across all models and organs, mean DSC was 0.79 (95% CI: 0.75-0.84). Mean DSC was highest for the kidney and bladder, each 0.91 (95% CI: 0.87-0.95), and lowest for the diaphragm at 0.63 (95% CI: 0.60-0.67). EVIT U-Net achieved the highest DSC for kidney, liver, and spleen, performed comparably to the highest-performing models for bladder, and had a mean inference time of 54 milliseconds per image. In previously unlabeled pediatric FAST clips, experts rated model-generated organ masks as acceptable for localization in 73%-95% of clips across organs. Conclusion: We describe the automatic segmentation of key abdominal organs in pediatric FAST with limited annotated data. This represents an important advancement in our image processing pipeline and can accelerate the development of large, robust datasets with segmentation for anatomy and pathology. Experts found that model-generated masks provided acceptable localization in most previously unlabeled pediatric clips, supporting the potential use of automated segmentation in pediatric FAST image analysis.

papers.title: Biopsy-Validated Deep Learning Mapping of Glioma Infiltration Beyond Contrast Enhancement Using Multiparametric MRI
papers.abstract: Background: Glioblastoma (GBM) exhibits diffuse tumor infiltration beyond contrast-enhancing margins into FLAIR-hyperintense brain tissue, where infiltrative tumor is not visible on conventional MRI. We developed and validated the infiltrative Tumor Burden (iTB) map, a deep learning biomarker that uses multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) to identify infiltrative tumor within these non-enhancing regions. Methods: Preoperative mpMRI datasets from 80 patients with WHO grade II-IV gliomas and 24 patients with brain metastases were retrospectively analyzed. Imaging included pre- and post-contrast T1-weighted, T2-weighted, FLAIR, dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion and diffusion MRI-derived maps (rCBV, rCBF, ADC). Spatially localized stereotactic biopsies from non-enhancing glioma regions provided histopathologic ground truth while peritumoral brain metastasis regions served as biologically grounded non-tumor controls. A 3D convolutional neural network was trained on voxel-centered mpMRI patches using patient-level cross-validation and an independent test set, with data augmentation optimized using a greedy local search strategy. Results: Model development included 121 biopsy-localized samples from 56 glioma patients and 104 non-tumor samples from 26 brain metastasis patients. Augmentation optimization significantly improved independent test-set performance, increasing accuracy from 74.5% to 85.5% and AUC from 0.859 to 0.942 (p = 0.008). Ensemble-derived voxel-wise iTB maps demonstrated low infiltration probabilities in brain metastases and extensive regions of elevated infiltration probability in glioblastoma, consistent with expected biology. Conclusions: The iTB biomarker generates voxel-wise maps of tumor infiltration within non-enhancing FLAIR abnormalities. Validated against image-localized histopathology and independent testing, it achieved high diagnostic performance and may improve surgical planning, radiotherapy targeting, and assessment of glioma burden.

papers.title: Divergence from Diffusion Tensor: a discriminant diffusion marker from single shell MRI
papers.abstract: Purpose: The Divergence from the Diffusion Tensor (DDT) is a new diffusion MRI metric that quantifies how the measured diffusion signal separates from the tensor assumption. It is marker for tissue heterogeneity that is estimated from single-shell data and can be used in brain studies. Methods: There exist other techniques that allow the calculation of how the measured diffusion diverges from the Gaussian and tensor assumptions. However, the calculation requires large data-sets with different b-values, which makes them incompatible which standard diffusion tensor acquisitions. By imposing an initial assumption, an alternative formulation based on one single shell (ie, single b-value) is reported. Results: Publicly available databases are used to test the behavior of DDT against other anisotropy measures. It shows the ability to discriminate different non-Gaussian diffusion scenarios with very low intra-subject variabilities. Conclusions: DDT can extract relevant information from the white matter, without any additional demands on data acquisition and totally compatible with standard diffusion MRI analysis pipelines. This makes DDT a good candidate to be used as an imaging marker for brain studies.

papers.title: Motion-robust high-resolution 3D-GRASE pseudo-continuous ASL perfusion imaging at 3T
papers.abstract: PurposeHigh resolution arterial spin labeling (ASL)-based perfusion imaging is desirable for many applications but suffers from low SNR and motion sensitivity due to the necessity for highly segmented readouts. Acquisition and reconstruction strategies were optimized for motionrobust high-resolution pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling (pCASL) of the brain at 3T using segmented 3D Gradient and Spin Echo (3D-GRASE) at 2.0-mm isotropic resolution. MethodsA high-resolution 3D-GRASE pCASL sequence was implemented at 3T and evaluated with a focus on the interaction between background suppression strength and motion-corrected reconstruction, together with the fat suppression and control-tag subtraction strategies that strong suppression requires. Motion correction was performed using a novel motion-compensated (alignedSENSE-based) reconstruction that simultaneously estimates the motion and image, accounting for contrast changes between tag and control data. Eight healthy volunteers were scanned under motion-free and cued motion conditions. Image quality was assessed against motion-free reference images using peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and a structural similarity index measure (SSIM). ResultsThe optimized acquisition-reconstruction pipeline enabled robust 2.0-mm isotropic pCASL at 3T and showed improved resistance to motion-related degradation. Strong BGS provided near-complete suppression of static tissue, and water excitation reduced lipid contamination and improved coil sensitivity estimation. The regularized alignedSENSE motion correction further improved perfusion-image quality, increasing SSIM by 18.7% under Strong BGS. ConclusionRobust high-resolution pCASL at 3T can be achieved through combined optimization of acquisition and reconstruction. The combination of Strong BGS, water excitation, reference-superimposed processing, and regularized motion correction mitigates motion-related degradation and yields higher-quality perfusion images for high-resolution ASL.

papers.title: Current gaps in downstream applications of fMRI foundation models: lessons learned from BrainLM & BrainHarmonix on Prevent-AD
papers.abstract: Foundation models have driven major advancements in the language and vision domains, as seen in the popularity of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, and a growing number of studies are bringing the approach to human brain imaging. Whether these models are ready for independent researchers to use on clinical datasets has yet to be examined. We evaluated two recent fMRI foundation models, BrainLM and BrainHarmonix, on PreventAD, a dataset on adults with a family history of Alzheimers disease. We compared features from frozen and fine-tuned models against two baselines: functional connectivity and a dummy classifier that always predicts the most common class. The sample includes 343 subjects who passed quality control, with a subset of 218 who had amyloid PET imaging. We tested four prediction targets: sex, age, progression to mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and {beta}-amyloid burden. Both models required substantial changes to the released code. BrainLMs own data preparation workflow did not produce stable fine-tuning, which we achieved only after switching to a standard workflow implemented with the library Nilearn. BrainHarmonixs documentation did not specify how to normalize new data, so we resolved this by testing different alternatives. For sex, functional connectivity outperformed all foundation model features. For age group, the best foundation model feature, taken from BrainHarmonixs structural (T1-weighted) encoder, slightly exceeded functional connectivity, but the difference was not significant. For MCI and {beta}-amyloid, no feature exceeded the dummy classifier in accuracy, and the area under the curve (AUC) stayed near chance for all features. For both clinical targets, the most precise feature came from fine-tuned BrainLM, meaning a larger share of its positive predictions were correct than for functional connectivity, but neither difference reached statistical significance. These results suggested that the strong transfer to new tasks seen in large language models cannot yet be assumed for fMRI foundation models, and that both models required code adaptation that would preclude their streamlined adoption by independent groups. We recommend that future studies provide standardized data workflows and always report functional connectivity and dummy classifier baselines. For clinical targets with strong class imbalance, studies should report several metrics, including precision.

papers.title: Training-free generation of 4D CT and other rare acquisitions improves segmentation across modalities
papers.abstract: RationaleRoutine clinical imaging captures anatomy under a limited set of physiologic and acquisition conditions, leaving segmentation models with sparse examples of how lesions and surrounding tissues deform with compression, respiration, or vascular pulsation. Standard image augmentation expands training datasets but does not explicitly model the mechanics underlying these changes. Patient-specific biomechanical simulation offers an approach to generate anatomically consistent images and corresponding segmentation masks under conditions absent from the original scan, without additional imaging or training a generative model. We hypothesized that incorporating this mechanistically grounded variability into training improves segmentation across imaging modalities. MethodsWe evaluate across three segmentation tasks: breast cancer on 3D digital breast tomosynthesis, lung tumors on chest CT, and carotid plaque on ultrasound. From each routine scan, patient-specific biomechanical models generate acquisitions absent from the original study--a range of breast compressions, the respiratory cycle, and arterial wall distension across the cardiac cycle. The resulting displacement fields deform both images and masks. Segmentation models were trained with and without the generated data across a range of standard image augmentation techniques, evaluated via cross-validation and held-out test sets. Realism was assessed through blinded reader studies, and generated respiratory motion was validated against real 4D CT. ResultsTraining on the generated acquisitions improved segmentation across modalities, increasing Dice scores by 6.6% for breast (p 0.05) relative to the routine scans alone. Generated respiratory motion closely matched real gated 4D CT, with Dice of 0.94 {+/-} 0.02 for lung volume overlap. Blinded readers discriminated generated from real images at near chance (AUC: breast 0.61, lung 0.41, carotid 0.46). ConclusionsMechanistic simulation generates imaging acquisitions that clinical systems do not supply, without training data or additional scanning, and improves AI-based disease detection across modalities.

papers.title: Usability and Physician Acceptance of AI in Chest Radiography: An Evaluation of the MeDeep Platform Using SUS and ATRAI-14
papers.abstract: ObjectivesArtificial intelligence (AI) architectures demonstrate high proficiency in chest radiography interpretation, yet successful clinical integration is often hampered by usability challenges and physician skepticism. This study evaluates the ergonomic usability and professional acceptance of the MeDeep AI platform among medical practitioners to identify key drivers of clinical trust. MethodsA multicenter, cross-sectional study was conducted across hospitals in Kermanshah, evaluating 88 medical professionals, including attending radiologists, radiology residents, internal medicine physicians, and medical externs. The System Usability Scale (SUS) was utilized to measure the platforms ergonomic functionality (n = 82), while the validated ATRAI-14 questionnaire quantified broader attitudes and trust regarding AI integration (n = 88). ResultsThe MeDeep platform achieved a high mean SUS score of 84.93, indicating excellent usability uniformly experienced across all professional subgroups (p = 0.387). However, overarching AI acceptance and algorithmic trust varied significantly by clinical role. Radiology residents exhibited significantly higher overarching AI acceptance (p = 0.016) and algorithmic trust (p = 0.008) compared to attending radiologists. Multivariate regression demonstrated that user familiarity (Beta = 0.500, p < 0.001) and perceived system usability (Beta = 0.236, p = 0.012)--rather than years of clinical experience--were the primary independent positive predictors of AI acceptance. Furthermore, higher perceived usability directly predicted greater algorithmic trust (Beta = 0.282, p = 0.009). ConclusionWhile technical usability is a necessary baseline for diagnostic platforms, professional trust dictates ultimate clinical adoption. Overcoming the generational divide in AI acceptance requires developers to prioritize intuitive interface design and position AI as a workflow-augmenting tool that addresses administrative burdens. Key PointsO_LIThe MeDeep AI platform demonstrated excellent ergonomic usability uniformly across all professional clinical ranks. C_LIO_LISignificant generational divides exist, with residents exhibiting higher algorithmic trust than attending radiologists. C_LIO_LIUser familiarity and perceived usability predict overarching AI acceptance better than years of clinical experience. C_LI

papers.title: Quantized TotalSegmentator for Fast Abdominal Organ Segmentation on CPUs
papers.abstract: BACKGROUNDTotalSegmentator is designed for a graphics processing unit (GPU), runs slowly on a central processing unit (CPU), and depends on Python, limiting CPU-only clinical deployment. OBJECTIVEThe purpose of this study was to evaluate whether TS-Portable, a self-contained CPU executable running 8-bit integer (INT8)-quantized TotalSegmentator models, is noninferior to the reference implementation across 15 abdominal organs in an external multicenter cohort, quantify CPU-only runtime, and demonstrate spleen volumetry on a picture archiving and communication system (PACS) reading station. METHODSThis retrospective study compared TS-Portable with the reference Python implementation on 100 external multicenter CT scans and 28 chronic liver disease series. Per-case mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and 3-mm normalized surface distance (NSD@3 mm) across 15 organs (1.5-mm resolution) and spleen-only mode were tested against a 0.01 noninferiority margin (paired bootstrap 95% CIs). Workstation and PACS runtimes were recorded; spleen volumes were compared via Lins concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) and Bland-Altman analysis. RESULTSThe external cohort included 100 patients (53 men, 47 women; mean age, 53 {+/-} 16 [SD] years). Across 15 organs, TS-Portable was noninferior for mean DSC (difference, 0.00017; 95% CI, 0.00003-0.00031; p < .001) and NSD@3 mm (difference, 0.00015; 95% CI, -0.00002 to 0.00031; p < .001) and in spleen-only mode (both p < .001). Workstation 1.5-mm median runtime was 48.0 seconds for TS-Portable on CPU versus 342.5 seconds on CPU (ratio, 7.14) and 61.5 seconds on GPU (ratio, 1.28) for the reference. On PACS, CPU spleen volumetry took 5.8 versus 43.4 seconds, agreeing with the reference (CCC, 0.9999; bias, 0.2%; 95% limits of agreement, -7.2% to 7.6%) and manual contours (CCC, 0.989; bias, -6.8%). In 28 chronic liver disease series, TS-Portable ran from DICOM in 6.5 seconds (median), agreeing with the reference (CCC, 0.99999) and manual contours (CCC, 0.992; bias, -3.4%). CONCLUSIONTS-Portable achieved noninferior abdominal organ segmentation accuracy compared with the reference implementation while running faster on a workstation CPU than the reference on a GPU. CLINICAL IMPACTSelf-contained deployment enables fast multiorgan segmentation on CPU-only computers and spleen volumetry within seconds on a standard reading station, without dedicated GPUs or software installation. HighlightsO_ST_ABSKey FindingC_ST_ABSAcross 100 external multicenter CT examinations, a quantized, self-contained CPU executable of TotalSegmentator was noninferior to the reference implementation for 15-organ segmentation accuracy and 7.14-fold faster on a workstation CPU, and completed reading-station spleen volumetry in a median of 5.8 seconds. ImportanceCompiling and quantizing three-dimensional segmentation models into a standalone CPU executable removes GPU and software-installation barriers, enabling rapid quantitative CT analysis on standard clinical workstations.

papers.title: Fine-tuned Medical Vision-Language Model (MedGemma 1.5 4B) with and without Structured Radiologist Descriptors versus EU-TIRADS for Malignancy Risk Stratification of Thyroid Nodules at Ultrasound: A Tunisian Multicenter Diagnostic Accuracy Study
papers.abstract: PurposeTo evaluate a medical vision-language foundation model fine-tuned on thyroid ultrasound images, with or without the radiologists structured descriptors, against expert-rated EU-TIRADS for the classification of thyroid nodules as benign or malignant. Materials and MethodsThis retrospective study included nodules that underwent ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) between January 2019 and August 2025 in two Tunisian centers, with consecutive recruitment, together with a selection of images from an international public dataset. Of 1,580 nodules, 1,456 (272 malignant; 1,280 patients) with an interpretable cytological or histological reference standard were allocated at patient level to training (n = 942), validation (n = 258) and a test set sealed before training (n = 256; 51 malignant). MedGemma 1.5 4B was fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation under four input configurations: the image with nodule biometry, with or without age and sex (A, B); A with chain-of-thought supervision (C); and A plus the eleven qualitative descriptors of the radiologists structured report (D). The EU-TIRADS category was never a model input. Areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) were compared with DeLongs test and a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.05; EU-TIRADS [≥] 4 was the prespecified comparator, with [≥] 5 as a sensitivity analysis. ResultsConfig D reached an AUROC of 0.953 (95% CI 0.909-0.976), versus 0.948 (0.894-0.972) for EU-TIRADS (difference +0.004, 95% CI -0.016 to +0.025), which met the non-inferiority criterion; Configs A-C, without the qualitative descriptors, reached 0.883-0.892 (Holm-adjusted p = 0.045 versus EU-TIRADS). At [≥] 4, EU-TIRADS had a sensitivity of 98.0% and produced 94 false positives among 205 benign nodules; at a threshold fixed on validation data, Config D reclassified 72 of them as negative while missing two additional cancers. Against EU-TIRADS [≥] 5 (sensitivity 92.2%, specificity 95.1%), Config D at its native threshold (88.2%, 94.1%) did not classify more nodules correctly (McNemar p = 0.22), and at its two other thresholds it classified fewer nodules correctly (p = 0.004 and 0.007). Raw probabilities were miscalibrated (expected calibration error 0.117 for Config D), and Platt scaling within the test set reduced this error to 0.019-0.040. ConclusionGiven the ultrasound image together with the radiologists structured descriptors, the fine-tuned model matched expert EU-TIRADS discrimination and, against the [≥] 4 threshold, reclassified most false positives as negative, a gain concentrated in category 4 and based on only three cancers in category 4. It is best positioned as a report-standardizing second reader in the EU-TIRADS 4 gray zone, pending prospective external validation. Summary StatementA fine-tuned medical vision-language model given the ultrasound image and the radiologists structured report matched expert EU-TIRADS discrimination of thyroid nodules and would have deferred most aspirations of benign category 4 nodules, at the cost of one or two missed category 4 cancers depending on the threshold, based on only three cancers in category 4. Key PointsO_LIOn a test set of 256 thyroid nodules sealed before training, the model given the ultrasound image and the radiologists 16-field structured report reached an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.953, non-inferior to expert EU-TIRADS (0.948). C_LIO_LIAgainst EU-TIRADS 4 or higher, the model reclassified as negative 72 of the 94 false-positive nodules at a threshold fixed on validation data, at the cost of two additional missed cancers. C_LIO_LIAdding the radiologists qualitative descriptors to the image raised the area under the curve from 0.892 (Config A) to 0.953, and Platt scaling reduced the calibration error of the model from 0.117 to 0.019-0.040. C_LI

papers.title: Feasibility study on using the diffusion-weighted imaging liver pulsation artifact as marker of liver fibrosis
papers.abstract: BackgroundLiver diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) often shows signal loss in the left lobe due to cardiac pulsation, known as the pulsation artifact. PurposeThis study was conducted to turn this bug into a feature. We hypothesized that the pulsation artifact, caused by mechanically transmitted waves, is influenced by tissue stiffness and, thereby, indicative of cirrhosis in the left liver lobe. Thus, we evaluated the potential of DWI pulsation artifacts to detect liver cirrhosis. Study typeThis study included both retrospective patients and prospective healthy volunteers. Study populationThirteen healthy volunteers, 16 patients with cirrhosis (Ishak 5 or 6), and three patients without cirrhosis (Ishak 0, 1, or 2) were included. Field Strength/SequenceImaging was performed at 1.5 T and 3 T using echoplanar DWI of the liver with two b-values, b50 = 50 s/mm{superscript 2} and b800 = 800 s/mm{superscript 2}. AssessmentAfter manual segmentation of the left and right liver lobes, 18 first-order features were extracted from b50 and b800 images. We assumed the pulsation artifact was predominantly present in the left liver lobe in the b800 images. Thus, we computed the ratios of the intensity-normalized b800 features obtained from the left and right liver lobes. Additionally, we performed an intensity normalization to address the sometimes different signal intensities of left and right liver lobe. Then, we conducted a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis to differentiate cirrhotic from non-cirrhotic livers. Statistical testsROC analysis and leave-one-out bootstrapping were applied, both yielding area under the curve (AUC) values. ResultsLeft liver pulsation artifacts were more pronounced in non-cirrhotic livers and largely absent in cirrhotic livers. The first quartile feature, i.e. the first quartile of the normalized signal, best distinguished cirrhotic from non-cirrhotic livers (AUC = 0.95; 95% confidence interval 0.87 - 1.00). Data conclusionThe left liver DWI pulsation artifact reflects liver stiffness and could serve as a simple, intrinsic marker of liver cirrhosis. Analysis of the signal magnitude can differentiate cirrhotic from non-cirrhotic livers.

papers.title: Ordinal Multi-Instance Learning for Automated Multi-Task Grading of Lumbar Degenerative Conditions on Sagittal MRI, with External Validation
papers.abstract: PurposeLumbar spine MRI interpretation requires 25 structured severity judgments per examination -- five degenerative conditions at five disc levels, each on a three-level ordinal scale -- a time-consuming task with substantial inter-reader variability. We developed and externally validated a model that automates this complete scheme. Materials and MethodsA full-sequence multi-instance learning (MIL) model -- ResNet34 backbone, bidirectional GRU, attention pooling over 24 uniformly sampled sagittal T2-weighted slices -- with 25 cumulative-logit ordinal heads was trained on 1,204 examinations from the multi-institutional RSNA 2024 LumbarDISC dataset and internally validated on 213 held-out examinations. External validation used 60 retrospectively collected patients from an independent Chinese university hospital (four scanner vendors, radiology reports as the reference standard, no fine-tuning). Agreement was assessed with exact accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, McNemar tests, and patient-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals. ResultsThe ordinal model achieved 51.4% balanced accuracy internally (exact accuracy 65.1%), versus 16.3% for a single-slice baseline; severe-grade AUCs averaged 0.908 across conditions. Externally, it outperformed its softmax-weighted counterpart on exact accuracy (0.649 vs. 0.586; +6.3 percentage points, 95% CI +2.7 to +10.0) and sensitivity (0.868 vs. 0.833), with markedly fewer severe-grade false alarms (69 vs. 172 predicted severe cells; McNemar p<0.0001). ConclusionA full-sequence MIL model with ordinal outputs automates the complete 25-task grading scheme on sagittal MRI and, in the first hospital external validation of such a model, reduced severe-grade over-prediction under domain shift without loss of sensitivity -- supporting its role as a screening and triage aid. SummaryAn ordinal full-sequence multi-instance learning model graded all 25 lumbar MRI degeneration tasks and markedly reduced severe-grade false alarms in 60-patient hospital validation without loss of sensitivity. Key PointsO_LIFull-sequence attention was indispensable: balanced accuracy rose from 16.3% (single-slice baseline) to 51.4% over 24 sagittal slices. C_LIO_LIIn external validation, ordinal outputs reduced severe-grade predictions from 172 to 69 of 900 cells (McNemar p<0.0001) with comparable ranking ability (AUC 0.835 vs. 0.829). C_LIO_LIThe Moderate grade remained the hardest class across all conditions (AUC 0.70-0.78), tracking known inter-reader variability at the mild-moderate boundary. C_LI

papers.title: Structural damage of the cervical spinal cord within and beyond the maximal compression area in mucopolysaccharidosis types I and VI
papers.abstract: BackgroundCervical spinal cord (CSC) compression and myelopathy are frequent, severe complications in mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS) types I and VI. Early detection is critical to prevent irreversible neurological deficits and preserve quality of life. This prospective study aimed to identify quantitative neuroimaging biomarkers of structural CSC damage and myelopathy in MPS I and VI. MethodsStructural and diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the CSC was analyzed in 17 MPS I patients, 3 MPS VI patients (19{+/-}7 years), and 19 case-matched healthy controls (20{+/-}7 years). CSC macrostructure (cross-sectional area, diameters) and microstructure (fractional anisotropy [FA], radial [RD], mean, axial diffusivities) were evaluated within and beyond the maximal compression areas. ResultsMPS patients demonstrated reduced CSC cross-sectional area and anterior-posterior diameter at upper cervical levels, alongside widespread microstructural alterations (lower FA, higher RD) throughout the CSC versus controls (pFDR<0.05). Restricted foramen magnum space was associated with microstructural damage at lower cervical levels without overt macrostructural compression. Morphological and microstructural metrics were sensitive to CSC compression and myelopathy severity (pFDR<0.05). Lower CSC integrity correlated with more advanced growth retardation (p<0.001). Among patients receiving hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, earlier treatment correlated with preserved upper CSC morphology (p<0.05). Distinct neuroimaging phenotypes were observed across MPS genotypes (pFDR<0.05). ConclusionsCSC MRI provides candidate neuroimaging biomarkers for early detection and characterization of myelopathy in MPS I and VI. Structural damage extends beyond primary maximal compression areas, highlighting these markers for clinical monitoring and future therapeutic trials.

papers.title: Discrepancies in Interpretation of Japanese Radiology Report Expressions Between Radiologists and Referring Physicians
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo evaluate discrepancies between radiologists and referring physicians in the interpretation of diagnostic probabilities conveyed by common Japanese expressions used in radiology reports. Materials and MethodsFifteen expressions commonly used to convey diagnostic probabilities in radiology reports were selected by five attending radiologists. An anonymous online survey was distributed to 26 radiologists and 33 referring physicians at a single institution. Participants assigned a diagnostic probability (from 0% to 100% in 10% increments) to each expression. Differences in median probabilities between radiologists and referring physicians were analyzed using the Mann-Whitney U test. Variability in interpretation was assessed using interquartile range (IQR), with IQR [≥] 30% defined as substantial variability. ResultsAll radiologists (26/26) and 97% of referring physicians (32/33) completed the survey. Seven of the 15 expressions showed statistically significant differences in interpretation between radiologists and referring physicians: "c/w" (80% vs. 60%; p = 0.031), the Japanese equivalents of "present" (100% vs. 100%; p = 0.024), "suspect of" (80% vs. 70%; p = 0.007), "possibly" (50% vs. 70%; p < 0.001), "unlikely" (10% vs. 10%; p = 0.022), "cannot be ruled out" (25% vs. 40%; p < 0.001), and "not inconsistent with" (80% vs. 90%; p = 0.008). Substantial variability in interpretation (IQR [≥] 30%) was observed for four expressions: "cannot be ruled out" (IQR, 10%-40%), "s/o" (IQR, 60%-90%), "c/w" (IQR, 50%-90%), and "not inconsistent with" (IQR, 70%-100%). ConclusionThis study revealed that nearly half of the Japanese expressions commonly used to convey diagnostic probabilities were interpreted differently by radiologists and referring physicians. These discrepancies highlight the need for a standardized lexicon to improve clarity and consistency in radiology reporting. Compliance with Reporting GuidelinesThis study was conducted in accordance with the STROBE guidelines for observational studies.

papers.title: Disagreement between AI and Radiologists: Quantifying Direction and Fragility
papers.abstract: BackgroundConventional performance metrics do not indicate whether artificial intelligence (AI)-platforms and radiologists are right or wrong on the same examinations, nor whether their non-agreement is more often beneficial or harmful. ObjectiveTo develop, illustrate, and apply directional metrics quantifying non-agreement between radiologists and AI-platforms against a common reference standard, and to adapt a fragility-based framework for quantifying the statistical robustness of these metrics. MethodsWe defined Positive Non-Agreement (PNA, AI-platform correct, radiologist incorrect), Negative Non-Agreement (NNA, radiologist correct, AI-platform incorrect), and Net Non-Agreement (NENA, their difference). Metrics were illustrated in three hypothetical scenarios of 1,000 examinations each and applied to three previously published AI-radiologist studies on pulmonary embolism and mammography. Bootstrap confidence intervals were calculated, and a reclassification fragility index (FI) quantified the minimum case reclassification needed to remove statistical support for NENAs direction. ResultsIn illustration, NENA was positive in two scenarios and negative in one. In the three published studies, NENA ranged from -4.18% to +10.74% and decreased consistently with increasing radiologist experience (junior residents, +6.27%; consultants, +1.45%), a gradient driven primarily by declining PNA with modest increase in NNA. The reclassification FI was defined for all three illustrative scenarios (range, 0.10%-1.70%) and for six of the seven comparisons from these studies (range, 0.34%-4.31%), but not for the weakest comparison, whose confidence interval for NENA included zero. ConclusionsPNA, NNA, and NENA provide a directional, case-level complement to conventional performance metrics for AI-radiologist non-agreement. The accompanying reclassification FI offers a statistically grounded, generalizable method for quantifying their robustness. Summary SentencePositive, Negative, and Net Non-Agreement, directional metrics developed and applied to published datasets comparing artificial intelligence with radiologists, show that the net benefit of artificial intelligence assistance depends on reader experience and clinical setting, and that the statistical robustness of these directional conclusions varies by comparison and sample size, which is information that conventional performance metrics alone do not provide. Key Points- Positive Non-Agreement (PNA), Negative Non-Agreement (NNA), and Net Non-Agreement (NENA) are directional metrics that identify whether AI-radiologist non-agreement is more likely to be beneficial or harmful, complementing conventional performance metrics to inform AI validation and monitoring decisions. - The reclassification fragility index (FI), anchored to statistical significance rather than to the point estimate, quantifies how many case reclassifications would remove support for the direction of NENA. - Applied to three previously published AI-radiologist datasets NENA ranged from -4.18% to +10.74% and fell from +6.27% to +1.45% with increasing radiologist experience, a gradient driven primarily by declining PNA with modest increase in NNA.

papers.title: Scaled m-BonacciNet: A Recurrence-Guided Lightweight CNN for Efficient Medical Image Classification
papers.abstract: The m-Bonacci weighted sequence space [Formula] is introduced for m [≥]2, 1[≤]p 0. It is proved to be a Banach space isometrically isomorphic to lp, with an unconditional Schauder basis. The space is also reflexive and uniformly convex. Its strict inclusion chain, continuous dual, and asymptotic truncation estimate of order[Formula] are established. Based on this framework, Scaled m-BonacciNet is proposed as a lightweight CNN that rescales Fibonacci-Net channels using the dominant m-Bonacci root and employs depthwise separable convolutions. Tribonacci-Net achieved 96.09% accuracy and 0.9581 macro F1-score on the 15-class Brain MRI dataset using 0.85 million parameters and 0.366 GFLOPs. Pentanacci-Net attained 95.87% accuracy on the 44-class dataset, reducing parameters and FLOPs by 47.10% and 44.48%. Hexanacci-Net achieved 83.75% accuracy and 0.7941 macro F1-score on CKD ultrasound.

papers.title: Morphometric Brain Networks at Ultra-Low Field: A First Assessment of Feasibility and Reliability
papers.abstract: BackgroundUltra-low field (ULF) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers accessible point-of-care neuroimag-ing, yet its capability to support multivariate network analyses remains understudied. MethodsWe systematically evaluated the feasibility and reliability of Morphometric Similarity Networks (MSN) and Morphometric Inverse Divergence (MIND) networks derived from paired high-field (HF, 3T/1.5T) and ULF (64mT) scans in a primary cohort (N=23) and an independent replication cohort (N=19). We tested the impact of super-resolution processing, cortical parcellation granularity (Desikan-Killiany vs. Destrieux), and mesh resolution (fsnative vs. fsaverage5) on edge-level cross-scanner agreement (Lins concordance correlation coefficient, CCC) and subject-level identifiability. ResultsMIND networks demonstrated higher edge-level HF-ULF agreement (mean CCC = 0.95) and ULF reproducibility (mean CCC = 0.98) compared to MSNs (mean CCC = 0.86-0.87 and 0.91-0.94, respectively). In contrast, MSNs yielded higher subject-level differential identifiability across field strengths due to a broader dis-tinction between within- and between-subject similarity. Reconstructing MIND networks on native high-resolution meshes (fsnative) maximised cross-scanner agreement, whereas coarser meshes and finer cortical parcellations enhanced individual network identifiability. ConclusionsStructural similarity networks can be reliably constructed from ULF MRI data. Optimal analytic choices depend on study objectives: MIND on native meshes maximises cross-scanner stability, whereas MSNs excel at preserving individual uniqueness, paving the way for globally scalable connectomic research.

papers.title: Clinical referral text overrides MRI evidence in multimodal large language models: glioma versus brain abscess
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo determine how strongly clinical referral text, rather than image content, drives the decisions of multimodal large language models (LLMs) differentiating glioma from brain abscess on MRI. Materials and methodsThis retrospective single-center study included 60 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted brain MRI examinations (30 gliomas, 30 abscesses; reference-standard diagnosis). One axial slice per case was paired with five referral texts (explicitly inflammatory to explicitly tumor-suggestive) under three prompt instructions and submitted 20 times each to GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, and Qwen 3.6 (72,000 answers). The primary outcome was the text-driven span (difference in tumor-call frequency between explicit inflammatory and explicit tumor text). Two blinded radiologists classified the images without text; sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were compared descriptively. ResultsPatients (29 women) had a mean age of 55.8 {+/-} 16.4 years. With neutral text, models answered tumor in 45-67% of queries (specificity, 0.38-0.78), versus 52% and 60% for radiologists (specificity, 0.77 and 0.63). The text-driven span was 0.79-1.00 (p < 0.001 for all models), whereas confirmed gliomas and abscesses differed by only 0.01-0.10 in three models and 0.25 in Gemini 3.5 Flash. Subtle wording produced at least 83% of the span in three models. An instruction to ignore the text reduced the span to 0.48-0.70 in three models and to 0.04 in Gemini 3.5 Flash, partly through reversion to a tumor default. Model accuracy was 0.52-0.73 versus 0.78 and 0.73 for radiologists. ConclusionMultimodal LLMs deferred to referral text over imaging evidence in differentiating glioma from brain abscess, and prompt instructions did not reliably correct this. Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSMultimodal large language models receive images together with clinical referral text, but how strongly the text rather than the image determines their diagnosis is unknown. FindingsChanging only the referral text largely reversed the glioma-versus-abscess decision for identical MRI images in four models; instructions to ignore the text reduced this inconsistently. Clinical relevanceBefore clinical use, multimodal large language models require model- and task-specific testing of their susceptibility to referral text, because instructing them to prioritize the image is not a dependable safeguard against text-driven misdiagnosis.

papers.title: Quantifying the Pharyngeal Wall Thickness on Modified Barium Swallow Studies: A Scoping Review and Reliability Study
papers.abstract: PurposePosterior pharyngeal wall (PPW) thickening is a common structural manifestation of treatment-related internal lymphedema in patients with head and neck cancer and can be evaluated using lateral videofluoroscopic images acquired during modified barium swallow (MBS) studies. However, no standardized method currently exists for quantitative measurement. MethodsThis two-phase methodological study first conducted a scoping review to characterize existing approaches to PPW thickness measurement and identify the principal factors contributing to variation in PPW thickness measurement. Eight studies were identified with variation observed across these measurement factors. An empirical reliability study was then performed using 107 MBS studies from 93 Head and Neck Cancer patients. Two independent raters annotated 10 anatomical landmarks on pre-swallow and post-swallow resting frames, and a computer-assisted algorithm quantitatively generated seven candidate PPW thickness measurements based on different vertebral reference points and measurement directions. Reliability was assessed intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). ResultsInter-rater reliability was highest for the measurement originating from the midpoint of C3 and extending perpendicular to the anterior C3 surface (ICC, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.72-0.83). Among the normalization references, C2-C4 vertebral length demonstrated greater reliability than C3 vertebral length, with an ICC of 0.88 (95% CI, 0.85-0.91). No significant differences were observed between pre-swallow and post-swallow PPW thickness measurements across the evaluated approaches. ConclusionsThese findings provide a methodological foundation for more standardized and reliable quantification of PPW thickness, with potential to expand the role of MBS from the functional evaluation of swallowing to include quantitative characterization of pharyngeal structural abnormalities.

papers.title: Evaluating the Interplay and Impact of Quality and Technical Variations on Performance of AI Models in Multi-Institutional Prostate MRI Datasets
papers.abstract: PurposeTo evaluate whether visually assessed high-quality prostate MRI, as defined by the Prostate Imaging Quality (PI-QUAL) scoring system, is sufficient to ensure consistent AI model performance, or whether hidden acquisition-related technical effects introduce variability that cannot be detected through visual inspection. MethodsThis retrospective study included 568 bpMRI scans from seven institutions, classified using PI-QUAL v2 into high-quality (scores 2-3) and low-quality (score 1) groups. Quantitative image quality features were extracted using MRQy from T2w and ADC sequences. Three experiments were conducted on high-quality scans: (1) unsupervised clustering to identify hidden technical batch effects; (2) V-Net models (M) for prostate capsule segmentation on T2w using single-cluster and balanced multi-cluster training strategies; and (3) VoxelMorph-based deformable registration (M2) to align ADC maps to T2w images. Performance metrics included DSC, precision, recall, volume ratio, HD95, ASSD, and TRE. Kruskal-Wallis tests assessed cross-cluster variability, Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) evaluated performance equivalence, and bootstrap resampling quantified training efficiency. ResultsClustering identified four clusters among 277 high-quality bpMRI scans. Single-cluster models showed variable performance (DSC=0.41-0.85) with significant batch effects (p<0.001), even with 140 training samples. The balanced multi-cluster model (n=60) eliminated batch effects (p=0.075), achieved equivalent performance (p<0.001), and demonstrated 2.23-fold greater training efficiency despite using 2.3-fold fewer samples. Registration performance also varied significantly across clusters (TRE=0.86-5.47 mm, p<0.001). ConclusionAcquisition-related batch effects significantly impact AI generalizability in prostate MRI, even among high-quality scans. Quantitative clustering enables detection of technical variations and supports diversity-aware training strategies that achieve equivalent performance with 2.3-fold fewer samples while eliminating batch effects. SummaryAcquisition-related batch effects significantly impair AI generalizability in prostate MRI, even among scans meeting PI-QUAL quality standards. Clustering-based diversity-aware training strategies successfully eliminated these batch effects and achieved 2.23-fold greater training efficiency compared to single-site approaches, demonstrating that strategic technical diversity outweighs dataset size for developing robust, clinically deployable AI models. Key PointsO_LIAcquisition-related batch effects significantly impair AI performance on prostate MRI, exceeding the impact of visual image quality as assessed by PI-QUAL scoring. C_LIO_LIEven the model trained on the largest single cluster exhibited significant batch effects (p<0.001). In contrast, a balanced multi-cluster model eliminated cross-cluster variability (p=0.075) while maintaining equivalent performance and requiring a smaller sample size. C_LIO_LIDiversity-aware training achieved 2.23-fold greater training efficiency (95% CI: 2.18-2.29) with 2.3-fold fewer samples, demonstrating that technical diversity outweighs data quantity for robust AI generalization. C_LI Clinical relevanceAddressing batch effects is essential for developing reliable, generalizable AI tools for prostate MRI interpretation.

papers.title: Vascular Proximity Coverage: A Novel CT-Based Marker of Pulmonary Vascular Distance to the Lung Parenchyma
papers.abstract: RationaleConventional CT-derived pulmonary vascular metrics quantify vascular pruning but do not assess spatial heterogeneity of vascular architecture. In COPD, peripheral microvascular pruning coexists with compensatory central vessel dilation, paradoxically preserving total vessel volume while reducing effective vascular penetration into lung parenchyma. ObjectivesTo develop and validate Vascular Proximity Coverage (VPC), a novel distance-based CT biomarker quantifying spatial efficiency of pulmonary vascular distribution. MethodsThis retrospective analysis included 7,881 COPDGene participants with complete vascular segmentations. VPC is estimated by integrating the area under the cumulative lung tissue coverage curve at distances 0-10 mm from segmented vessel voxels. Multivariable models were used to assess associations with lung function, six-minute walk distance (6MWD), St. Georges Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ), mMRC dyspnea score and all-cause mortality adjusting for demographics, smoking, emphysema, scanner type, and BV5. We stratified the cohort into four groups defined by the median values of BV5 and VPC, yielding discordant (high-BV5/low-VPC, low-BV5/high-VPC) and concordant (high/high, low/low) vascular phenotypes. ResultsVPC declined across disease severity (5.82 {+/-} 0.50 in non-smokers to 5.21 {+/-} 0.64 in GOLD 4; p<0.001). Among spirometrically normal smokers, current smokers showed reduced VPC versus former smokers (5.31 vs. 5.68; p<0.001). Each standard deviation (SD) decrease in VPC was independently associated with reduced 6MWD ({beta}=-16.8 m, 95% CI: -19.5 to -14.0), worse SGRQ ({beta}=1.9, 95% CI: 1.4 to 2.4), and increased dyspnea (RR=1.05, 95% CI: 1.03-1.08; all p<0.001). The lowest VPC quartile, as compared to the reference quartile, was associated with 38% higher mortality (HR=1.38, 95% CI: 1.18-1.62; p<0.001). Based on median thresholds, high-BV5/low-VPC phenotype, compared to High-BV5/High-VPC, showed 24% increased mortality (HR=1.24, 95% CI: 1.08-1.42; p=0.002) despite preserved vessel volume. ConclusionsVPC captures spatial heterogeneity of vascular architecture independent of vessel volume and detects subclinical vascular dysfunction in smokers without airflow obstruction. AT A GLANCE COMMENTARYO_ST_ABSScientific Knowledge on the SubjectC_ST_ABSCurrent CT-based pulmonary vascular metrics, including volume of blood vessels less than 5 mm{superscript 2} cross-sectional area (BV5) and total vessel volume, quantify the amount of visible vasculature but do not assess how effectively vessels reach the lung parenchyma for efficient gas exchange. In COPD, peripheral microvascular pruning commonly coexists with compensatory central vessel dilation, leading to preserved or increased total vascular volume despite compromised functional vascular distribution. What This Study Adds to the FieldVascular Proximity Coverage (VPC) is a novel distance-based CT biomarker that quantifies the spatial efficiency of pulmonary vascular distribution by measuring cumulative lung tissue coverage across distances from vessel walls. In 7,881 COPDGene participants, including non-smokers and PRISm subjects, lower VPC was independently associated with decreased lung function, reduced exercise capacity, worsened quality of life, and increased all-cause mortality over a median 10.8-year follow-up after adjusting for BV5 and emphysema. VPC identified a high-risk phenotype with preserved vessel volume but impaired distribution (high-BV5/low-VPC) that carried 24% increased mortality risk and detected subclinical vascular dysfunction in smokers with normal spirometry.

papers.title: Deep Learning-Based Anatomical Level Classification of Craniofacial CT Slices: Comparison of CNN Architectures and Ensemble Methods
papers.abstract: Computed tomography (CT) interpretation requires recognition of the anatomical level of each slice. Classification may facilitate preprocessing and AI-assisted fracture diagnosis. We developed deep learning models to classify craniofacial CT slices into six anatomical categories. A total of 11,769 images were collected from a multicenter database involving 10 Japanese university hospitals and the public Head-Neck-Radiomics-HN1 dataset. Patients were divided into training (70%) and evaluation (30%) sets. Five CNN architectures were trained from scratch, and hard- and soft-voting ensembles were evaluated. Individual-model accuracy ranged from 94.72% to 96.09%; the hard-voting ensemble achieved 96.46% accuracy (Cohens {kappa} = 0.954). Although performance differed among individual models (Cochrans Q = 99.29, p < 0.001), the ensemble did not significantly outperform EfficientNetV2B1 (McNemars p = 0.163). Errors occurred mainly between adjacent anatomical regions. Deep learning can classify craniofacial CT slices accurately and may support automated dataset organization and AI-assisted fracture diagnosis. External validation is needed.

papers.title: Neurochemical fingerprinting of the Alzheimers disease continuum using 7 T short-echo-time brain single voxel 1H-MRS.
papers.abstract: IntroductionThis study aimed to characterize the neurochemical profile of Alzheimers disease (AD) continuum stages using proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS) data for brain metabolites and macromolecules. We used Orthogonal Projection to Latent Structures Discriminant Analysis (OPLS-DA) to classify diagnostic groups and assess feature importance. MethodsOur dataset consisted of 7 T short-echo time 1H-MRS spectra of the posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus of individuals diagnosed with AD (n = 27) or Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI, n = 27) and Healthy Controls (HC, n = 31). Classification used 100-round Monte Carlo cross-validation based on metabolite concentrations and macromolecular peak intensities. Variable importance in projection (VIP) was assessed across classification models to identify the most relevant neurochemical features. The resulting metabolite rankings were compared with previous literature to evaluate their biological plausibility. ResultsClassification was strongest for AD versus HC (AUC=0.88) and lower for comparisons involving MCI. Metabolites contributing most strongly to classification included myo-inositol, ascorbate, and choline-containing compounds, consistent with previous studies on AD-related neurochemical alterations. In addition, specific macromolecular components were identified as relevant features, suggesting a potential contribution of MM signals to the characterization of AD-related neurochemistry. DiscussionThese findings support the use of short-echo-time 1H-MRS as a complementary tool for characterizing neurochemical changes in the AD continuum, with potential applications in disease characterization and monitoring, warranting validation in larger cohorts.

papers.title: Estimating the correlation between rates of change in longitudinal studies in presence of dropout
papers.abstract: Estimating the correlation between subject-specific rates of change is a common objective in longitudinal studies. A natural approach is to fit ordinary least squares regressions per subject and correlate the resulting slope estimates directly. Under complete data, this slopes-first estimator is algebraically equivalent to a contrast-based plug-in estimator derived from the joint variance-covariance matrix of the two signals across time. Under independent dropout, however, the slopes-first approach implicitly applies heterogeneous weights across missing-data patterns, introducing bias whenever the cross-covariance between the two signals is not constant over time. We formalise this result and propose an unbiased alternative that estimates the joint covariance matrix before applying the contrast. We further extend our results to include covariates as well. Simulations confirm that the slopes-first estimator is biased under non-constant cross-covariance while the proposed alternative remains unbiased. Further, we show in a real-world example that the two estimators can lead to different scientific conclusions and recommend that researchers working with longitudinal data inspect the missing data pattern to make an informed decision about the estimator of choice.

papers.title: Quantitative proton density mapping with data-driven reception profile correction derived from macromolecular proton fraction
papers.abstract: PurposeProton density (PD) and macromolecular proton fraction (MPF) are fundamental MR parameters characterizing water and macromolecular content in tissues. Both parameters can be mapped using a time-efficient MRI protocol, though PD maps require additional corrections for the reception profile (RP) non-uniformity and global scaling. Existing PD mapping methods suffer from uncertainties related to PD normalization to reference tissue. This study aimed to develop a data-driven RP correction method for PD mapping based on MPF as an internal scale. Theory and MethodsOne-parameter model linking PD and MPF was derived under assumption of proportionality between total macromolecular volume and proton concentration. This model with a uniform parameter value across brain tissues generates a surrogate PD map, which is used to estimate RP from an uncorrected PD map. The proposed algorithm was tested against a common PD mapping method utilizing bias-field correction and normalization to cerebrospinal fluid. Brain MRI data were acquired at 3T from seven healthy individuals. The protocol included 3D multi-echo T1-, PD-, and magnetization-transfer-weighted gradient-echo sequences. Parametric maps were reconstructed using the single-point MPF mapping algorithm with data-driven B1 correction. ResultsMPF-based and bias-field corrections yielded similar PD measurements in white and gray matter with no significant bias and remarkably small variability (coefficients of variation <0.6%). ConclusionsMPF-based RP correction enables computationally simple and robust quantitative PD mapping at no additional cost if MPF maps are available. The main advantage of the proposed method is automatic elimination of global scaling that obviates the need for PD normalization.

papers.title: Calibration, Uncertainty, and Data Efficiency of Deep Learning Chest Radiograph Classifiers Under Cross-Dataset Distribution Shift: A Multi-Dataset Benchmark
papers.abstract: PurposeTo evaluate the external transportability of source-derived probability calibration for chest radiograph deep learning classifiers under distribution shift and determine its dependence on sample size and disease prevalence. Materials and MethodsThis retrospective secondary computational analysis of public, de-identified radiographic datasets involved no participant contact or new data collection. Cohort sizes were prespecified by availability without prospective power calculation: 106,686 NIH ChestX-ray14 images (29,323 patients; 1992-2015) for development and internal testing, 20,000 CheXpert images (20,000 patients; October 2002-July 2017), and 14,998 VinBigData images (2018-2020) for external testing. ResNet-18, DenseNet-121, and DeiT-Tiny classifiers for cardiomegaly and pleural effusion were trained across four patient fractions and three seeds (36 fits). Calibrators were fitted exclusively on NIH data. Twelve primary external Brier-score contrasts (temperature-scaled versus raw probabilities) were evaluated using paired cluster-bootstrapping with Holm adjustment. ResultsTemperature scaling reduced Brier scores in nine of 12 primary contrasts but worsened pleural effusion calibration on VinBigData across all architectures (Brier increases: ResNet-18, 0.001460 [95% CI: 0.001347, 0.001568]; DenseNet-121, 0.001193 [95% CI: 0.001109, 0.001274]; DeiT-Tiny, 0.000498 [95% CI: 0.000417, 0.000577]; all adjusted P=.006). Standardizing class weights to NIH prevalence reversed all CheXpert improvements. Although full versus 10% training improved external AUROC across all comparisons, DeiT-Tiny CheXpert pleural effusion Brier score worsened by 0.007039 despite a 0.032466 AUROC gain. At 80% selective image retention, calibrated ensembles retained only 12.3%-17.2% of VinBigData positive pleural effusion examinations. ConclusionSource-fitted calibration is not uniformly transportable across health systems, and discrimination gains do not guarantee calibrated probabilities. External evaluation must simultaneously assess probability reliability, prevalence shifts, and retained-case composition.

papers.title: Deep Learning and Radiomics Models for Predicting 90-Day Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: BackgroundAccurate prediction of 90-day outcomes following ischemic stroke is crucial for optimizing clinical strategies. This study aimed to systematically review and meta-analyze studies using deep learning (DL) and hand-crafted radiomics (HCR) models for predicting 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) outcomes after ischemic stroke. MethodsWe followed the PRISMA guidelines for systematic reviews. Four databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library) were searched comprehensively for studies published up to September 2025. Inclusion criteria encompassed original research focusing on ischemic stroke patients with mRS at 90 days as the primary outcome and predictive models utilizing imaging biomarkers from CT or MRI. Quality assessment of the included studies was conducted using the PROBAST and and METhodological RadiomICs Score (METRICS) tools. ResultsSeventeen studies were included in the quantitative meta-analysis. Models demonstrated good prognostic performance for 90-day outcomes, with pooled AUCs of 0.85 (95% CI: 0.80-0.86) for internal and 0.74 (95% CI: 0.67-0.89) for external validation sets, with no significant difference (p=0.42). Deep learning and hand-crafted radiomics models showed comparable diagnostic accuracy in the primary analysis (p=0.667); a difference in sensitivity favouring hand-crafted radiomics emerged only in a post-hoc analysis after exclusion of one outlier study. Models incorporating clinical variables significantly outperformed imaging-only models (p<0.01). CT- and MRI-based models showed similar performance. Treatment-specific analyses revealed higher sensitivity for IVT-based models and higher specificity for combined MT+IVT models. ConclusionsDL and HCR models demonstrate robust potential for predicting 90-day outcomes in ischemic stroke. Future research should focus on standardizing model evaluation metrics and incorporating explainable AI techniques to improve clinical applicability.
